Lecture 15

Complex differentiability and analytic functions

Lecture objectives

We define the complex derivative and analytic functions and derive the Cauchy–Riemann equations, which are necessary and, with continuous partial derivatives, sufficient. We show that the real and imaginary parts are harmonic when they are C2,C^2C2, that their level curves are orthogonal where f′≠0,f'\ne0f′=0, and we reconstruct an analytic function from its real part.

Part I differentiated functions of a real variable. Some of them had complex values, such as eλt\ee^{\lambda t}eλt with λ∈C,\lambda\in\Cλ∈C, and GM 16 defined their derivative with a real increment of t.tt. Part II studies functions of a complex variable z,zz, whose derivative uses a complex increment that can approach zero from every direction in the plane. This one requirement implies the Cauchy–Riemann equations for the real and imaginary parts. When these parts are twice continuously differentiable, they are harmonic, like the logarithmic temperature profile in the cylindrical shell of Lecture 2. Branches, integrals, series and residues follow in Lectures 16–21.

Definition 15.1 (Domain). A domain is a nonempty open set U⊂CU\subset\CU⊂C that is polygonally connected.

15.2 The complex derivative

The derivative of a function of a complex variable is defined by the same difference quotient as for a real variable. The increment hhh is now a complex number.

Definition 15.2 (Complex derivative and analytic function). Let U⊂CU\subset\CU⊂C be open, let f:U→Cf:U\to\Cf:U→C and let z0∈U.z_0\in Uz0​∈U. The function fff is complex differentiable at z0z_0z0​ if the limit f′(z0)=lim⁡h→0f(z0+h)−f(z0)hf'(z_0)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(z_0+h)-f(z_0)}{h}f′(z0​)=h→0lim​hf(z0​+h)−f(z0​)​(15.1) exists, where hhh runs through the nonzero complex numbers with z0+h∈U.z_0+h\in Uz0​+h∈U. The function fff is analytic on UUU if it is complex differentiable at every point of U.UU. It is analytic at z0z_0z0​ if it is analytic on some disc Br(z0).B_r(z_0)Br​(z0​). An entire function is a function analytic on C.\CC.

Many texts say holomorphic for analytic. Lecture 18 shows that a function analytic on UUU is the sum of a convergent power series near each point of U,UU, which explains the name.

The limit (15.1) is a limit in the plane. The quotient must approach the same number f′(z0)f'(z_0)f′(z0​) along every line and every curve on which hhh tends to zero.

As for real functions, fff is complex differentiable at z0z_0z0​ with f′(z0)=af'(z_0)=af′(z0​)=a exactly when f(z0+h)=f(z0)+ah+r(h),r(h)h→0(h→0).f(z_0+h)=f(z_0)+ah+r(h),\qquad \frac{r(h)}{h}\to0\quad(h\to0).f(z0​+h)=f(z0​)+ah+r(h),hr(h)​→0(h→0).(15.2) Indeed, (15.2) defines r(h),r(h)r(h), and r(h)/hr(h)/hr(h)/h is the difference quotient minus a.aa. Since ∣f(z0+h)−f(z0)∣≤∣a∣∣h∣+∣r(h)∣→0,\abs{f(z_0+h)-f(z_0)}\le\abs a\abs h+\abs{r(h)}\to0,∣f(z0​+h)−f(z0​)∣≤∣a∣∣h∣+∣r(h)∣→0, a function complex differentiable at z0z_0z0​ is continuous at z0.z_0z0​.

15.3 The Cauchy–Riemann equations

We now express complex differentiability through the partial derivatives ux,u_xux​, uy,u_yuy​, vxv_xvx​ and vyv_yvy​ of GM 36. Approaching along the two axes gives a necessary condition.

GM 36 shows that continuous partial derivatives make a map differentiable. Together with Theorem 15.7 this gives the test used in practice.

Proposition 15.8 (A sufficient condition). Let U⊂CU\subset\CU⊂C be open, and let uuu and vvv be C1C^1C1 on U,UU, that is, let their four first partial derivatives exist and be continuous on U.UU. If the Cauchy–Riemann equations hold at every point of U,UU, then f=u+ivf=u+\iu vf=u+iv is analytic on U,UU, and f′=ux+ivxf'=u_x+\iu v_xf′=ux​+ivx​ is continuous on U.UU.

Proof. By the continuity criterion of GM 36, F=(u,v)F=(u,v)F=(u,v) is differentiable at every point of U.UU. Theorem 15.7 then shows that fff is complex differentiable at every point, with f′=ux+ivxf'=u_x+\iu v_xf′=ux​+ivx​ by Proposition 15.6. This function is continuous because its real and imaginary parts are. ■

Example 15.9 (The exponential and the trigonometric functions). We show that ez,\ee^zez, cos⁡z\cos zcosz and sin⁡z\sin zsinz are entire and compute their derivatives. Example 15.10 (Complex differentiable only on a line). Let f(x+iy)=x2+iy2f(x+\iu y)=x^2+\iu y^2f(x+iy)=x2+iy2 on C.\CC. 15.4 The Cauchy–Riemann equations in polar form

Rotations and radial fields are described more simply in polar coordinates z=reiθz=r\ee^{\iu\theta}z=reiθ with r>0r>0r>0 (GM 15–16). Let UUU be an open set with 0∉U.0\notin U0∈/U. At a point z=reiθ∈U,z=r\ee^{\iu\theta}\in Uz=reiθ∈U, the Cauchy–Riemann equations hold if and only if ur=1r vθ,vr=−1r uθ.u_r=\frac1r\,v_\theta,\qquad v_r=-\frac1r\,u_\theta .ur​=r1​vθ​,vr​=−r1​uθ​.(15.7) In that case f′(z)=e−iθ(ur+ivr).f'(z)=\ee^{-\iu\theta}(u_r+\iu v_r)f′(z)=e−iθ(ur​+ivr​).

15.5 Harmonic functions and orthogonal level curves

The Cauchy–Riemann equations couple uuu and v.vv. Eliminating one of them gives a single equation for the other.

Definition 15.14 (Harmonic function). Let U⊂R2U\subset\R^2U⊂R2 be open. A real function ψ\psiψ that is C2C^2C2 on UUU is harmonic on UUU if ∇2ψ=ψxx+ψyy=0on U.\laplacian\psi=\psi_{xx}+\psi_{yy}=0\quad\text{on }U.∇2ψ=ψxx​+ψyy​=0on U.(15.9)

This is Laplace’s equation in the plane, with ∇2=∂x2+∂y2,\laplacian=\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2∇2=∂x2​+∂y2​, the sign used throughout the course. In plane problems, steady temperatures without heat sources and electrostatic potentials without charges are harmonic.

Proposition 15.15 (Harmonic parts). Let f=u+ivf=u+\iu vf=u+iv be analytic on an open set U,UU, and let uuu and vvv be C2C^2C2 on U.UU. Then uuu and vvv are harmonic on U.UU.

Proof. Differentiate the Cauchy–Riemann equations ux=vyu_x=v_yux​=vy​ and uy=−vxu_y=-v_xuy​=−vx​ with respect to xxx and y,yy, respectively: uxx=vyx,uyy=−vxy.u_{xx}=v_{yx},\qquad u_{yy}=-v_{xy}.uxx​=vyx​,uyy​=−vxy​. Here vyxv_{yx}vyx​ denotes (vy)x,(v_y)_x(vy​)x​, the derivative first in yyy and then in x.xx. By Schwarz’s theorem (GM 37), vxy=vyxv_{xy}=v_{yx}vxy​=vyx​ for a C2C^2C2 function, so uxx+uyy=0.u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0uxx​+uyy​=0. In the same way vxx=−uyxv_{xx}=-u_{yx}vxx​=−uyx​ and vyy=uxy,v_{yy}=u_{xy}vyy​=uxy​, so vxx+vyy=0.v_{xx}+v_{yy}=0vxx​+vyy​=0. ■

Lecture 17 removes the hypothesis that uuu and vvv are C2.C^2C2. It shows, with Goursat’s theorem, that the derivative of an analytic function is again analytic, so uuu and vvv have continuous partial derivatives of every order.

Proposition 15.16 (Zero derivative). Let fff be analytic on a domain UUU with f′=0f'=0f′=0 on U.UU. Then fff is constant on U.UU.

Proof. By Proposition 15.6, f′=ux+ivx=vy−iuy.f'=u_x+\iu v_x=v_y-\iu u_yf′=ux​+ivx​=vy​−iuy​. Hence all four partial derivatives vanish on U.UU. In particular uuu and vvv are C1C^1C1 with zero gradients. Let z1,z2∈U,z_1,z_2\in Uz1​,z2​∈U, and join them by a polygonal path in U.UU. By the gradient endpoint formula of GM 40, u(z2)−u(z1)u(z_2)-u(z_1)u(z2​)−u(z1​) is the integral of ∇u=0\grad u=0∇u=0 along this path, so u(z2)=u(z1).u(z_2)=u(z_1)u(z2​)=u(z1​). The same holds for v.vv. ■

The level curves of uuu and vvv are the curves on which uuu or vvv is constant. For a temperature uuu they are the isotherms.

Proposition 15.17 (Orthogonal gradients). Let f=u+ivf=u+\iu vf=u+iv be analytic on an open set UUU with uuu and vvv of class C1,C^1C1, and let z0∈Uz_0\in Uz0​∈U with f′(z0)≠0.f'(z_0)\ne0f′(z0​)=0. Then at z0z_0z0​ ∇u⋅∇v=0,∥∇u∥=∥∇v∥=∣f′(z0)∣≠0.\grad u\cdot\grad v=0,\qquad \norm{\grad u}=\norm{\grad v}=\abs{f'(z_0)}\ne0 .∇u⋅∇v=0,∥∇u∥=∥∇v∥=∣f′(z0​)∣=0.(15.10)

Proof. By the Cauchy–Riemann equations, ∇u=(ux,uy)=(ux,−vx)\grad u=(u_x,u_y)=(u_x,-v_x)∇u=(ux​,uy​)=(ux​,−vx​) and ∇v=(vx,vy)=(vx,ux).\grad v=(v_x,v_y)=(v_x,u_x)∇v=(vx​,vy​)=(vx​,ux​). Hence ∇u⋅∇v=uxvx−vxux=0,∥∇u∥2=∥∇v∥2=ux2+vx2=∣f′(z0)∣2.\grad u\cdot\grad v=u_xv_x-v_xu_x=0,\qquad \norm{\grad u}^2=\norm{\grad v}^2=u_x^2+v_x^2=\abs{f'(z_0)}^2 .∇u⋅∇v=ux​vx​−vx​ux​=0,∥∇u∥2=∥∇v∥2=ux2​+vx2​=∣f′(z0​)∣2.■

We now turn to the level sets {z∈U:u(z)=u(z0)},{z∈U:v(z)=v(z0)}.\{z\in U:u(z)=u(z_0)\},\qquad \{z\in U:v(z)=v(z_0)\}.{z∈U:u(z)=u(z0​)},{z∈U:v(z)=v(z0​)}. Since ∇u(z0)≠0,\grad u(z_0)\ne0∇u(z0​)=0, one of its partial derivatives is nonzero. The implicit function theorem, which GM 37 cites, applied with that coordinate as the dependent variable, shows that near z0z_0z0​ the level set of uuu is the graph of a C1C^1C1 function, a curve whose normal at z0z_0z0​ is ∇u(z0).\grad u(z_0)∇u(z0​). The same holds for v.vv. Hence the two level curves cross at z0z_0z0​ at a right angle.

Let f′(z0)≠0.f'(z_0)\ne0f′(z0​)=0. By Proposition 15.5, a curve through z0z_0z0​ with velocity z′(t0)≠0z'(t_0)\ne0z′(t0​)=0 is mapped by fff to a curve with the nonzero velocity f′(z0)z′(t0).f'(z_0)z'(t_0)f′(z0​)z′(t0​). Every velocity is rotated by the same angle, an argument of f′(z0),f'(z_0)f′(z0​), and stretched by the same factor ∣f′(z0)∣.\abs{f'(z_0)}∣f′(z0​)∣. Hence two curves through z0z_0z0​ cross at the same angle as their images. A map with this property is called conformal at z0.z_0z0​. With w=f(z),w=f(z)w=f(z), the level curves of uuu and vvv are mapped to the lines Re⁡w=const\Re w=\text{const}Rew=const and Im⁡w=const\Im w=\text{const}Imw=const of the image plane, which cross at a right angle.

Example 15.18 (The level curves of z2).z^2z2). Let f(z)=z2,f(z)=z^2f(z)=z2, with u=x2−y2,u=x^2-y^2u=x2−y2, v=2xyv=2xyv=2xy and f′(z)=2z.f'(z)=2zf′(z)=2z. Figure 15.1 shows the level curves. Away from the origin u=ku=ku=k and v=kv=kv=k with k≠0k\ne0k=0 are hyperbolas, and each hyperbola of one family crosses each hyperbola of the other at a right angle. At the origin f′(0)=0,f'(0)=0f′(0)=0, and the hypothesis of Proposition 15.17 fails. The level set u=0u=0u=0 is the pair of lines y=±x,y=\pm xy=±x, the level set v=0v=0v=0 is the pair of axes, and these lines cross at the angle π/4.\pi/4π/4. The map z↦z2z\mapsto z^2z↦z2 doubles the angles at the origin, so it is not conformal there. ◃

15.6 Harmonic conjugates

In a plane problem one usually knows a harmonic function, such as a temperature or a potential, and wants the analytic function whose real part it is. Its imaginary part has a name of its own.

Definition 15.19 (Harmonic conjugate). Let uuu be harmonic on an open set U⊂C.U\subset\CU⊂C. A real function vvv on UUU is a harmonic conjugate of uuu if u+ivu+\iu vu+iv is analytic on U.UU.

The word is unrelated to the complex conjugate z‾.\conj zz. On a domain a harmonic conjugate is unique up to an additive real constant. Indeed, let v1v_1v1​ and v2v_2v2​ be two of them and w=v1−v2.w=v_1-v_2w=v1​−v2​. The difference g=iwg=\iu wg=iw of the two analytic functions is analytic, with real part 000 and imaginary part w.ww. The Cauchy–Riemann equations for ggg give wy=0w_y=0wy​=0 and wx=0,w_x=0wx​=0, so g′=iwx=0,g'=\iu w_x=0g′=iwx​=0, and ggg is constant by Proposition 15.16.

Existence depends on the shape of the set. As in GM 40, a set UUU is star-shaped about z∗∈Uz_*\in Uz∗​∈U if the segment from z∗z_*z∗​ to every point of UUU lies in U.UU. Discs, half-planes and the whole plane are star-shaped about each of their points. The cut plane C∖(−∞,0]\C\setminus(-\infty,0]C∖(−∞,0] is star-shaped about 1,11, because the segment from 111 to any of its points meets the real axis only in positive numbers.

Theorem 15.20 (Harmonic conjugate on a star-shaped set). Let U⊂CU\subset\CU⊂C be open and star-shaped about z∗∈U,z_*\in Uz∗​∈U, and let uuu be harmonic on U.UU. Then uuu has a harmonic conjugate vvv on U,UU, and vvv is C2.C^2C2. Every other harmonic conjugate is v+cv+cv+c with a real constant c.cc.

Proof. Consider the plane vector field F=(F1,F2)=(−uy,ux).\vv F=(F_1,F_2)=(-u_y,u_x)F=(F1​,F2​)=(−uy​,ux​). It is C1C^1C1 on U,UU, because uuu is C2,C^2C2, and its cross partials agree: ∂xF2−∂yF1=uxx+uyy=0.\partial_xF_2-\partial_yF_1=u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0 .∂x​F2​−∂y​F1​=uxx​+uyy​=0. By the potential theorem of GM 40 on star-shaped sets, there is a C1C^1C1 function vvv on UUU with ∇v=F,\grad v=\vv F∇v=F, that is, vx=−uy,vy=ux.v_x=-u_y,\qquad v_y=u_x .vx​=−uy​,vy​=ux​. These are the Cauchy–Riemann equations. Since uuu and vvv are C1,C^1C1, Proposition 15.8 shows that u+ivu+\iu vu+iv is analytic on U.UU. The partial derivatives of vvv are C1,C^1C1, so vvv is C2.C^2C2. A star-shaped set is polygonally connected (GM 40), so UUU is a domain, and uniqueness up to a constant was shown above. ■

In practice we integrate one Cauchy–Riemann equation and fix the remaining function with the other.

Example 15.21 (Reconstructing an analytic function from its real part). Let u(x,y)=e−ycos⁡x+xy((x,y)∈R2).u(x,y)=\ee^{-y}\cos x+xy\qquad\bigl((x,y)\in\R^2\bigr).u(x,y)=e−ycosx+xy((x,y)∈R2). We show that uuu is harmonic, find its harmonic conjugate vvv with v(0,0)=0,v(0,0)=0v(0,0)=0, and write f=u+ivf=u+\iu vf=u+iv as a function of z.zz.

First, uuu is C2,C^2C2, with uxx=−e−ycos⁡xu_{xx}=-\ee^{-y}\cos xuxx​=−e−ycosx and uyy=e−ycos⁡x.u_{yy}=\ee^{-y}\cos xuyy​=e−ycosx. Hence uuu is harmonic on the plane, which is star-shaped, and Theorem 15.20 guarantees a conjugate. The partial derivatives are ux=−e−ysin⁡x+y,uy=−e−ycos⁡x+x.u_x=-\ee^{-y}\sin x+y,\qquad u_y=-\ee^{-y}\cos x+x .ux​=−e−ysinx+y,uy​=−e−ycosx+x. Next, integrate the equation vy=uxv_y=u_xvy​=ux​ with respect to yyy at fixed x:xx: v(x,y)=e−ysin⁡x+12y2+g(x),v(x,y)=\ee^{-y}\sin x+\tfrac12y^2+g(x),v(x,y)=e−ysinx+21​y2+g(x), where ggg is a function of xxx alone. The other equation vx=−uyv_x=-u_yvx​=−uy​ requires e−ycos⁡x+g′(x)=e−ycos⁡x−x,\ee^{-y}\cos x+g'(x)=\ee^{-y}\cos x-x,e−ycosx+g′(x)=e−ycosx−x, so g′(x)=−xg'(x)=-xg′(x)=−x and g(x)=−12x2+c.g(x)=-\tfrac12x^2+cg(x)=−21​x2+c. The condition v(0,0)=0v(0,0)=0v(0,0)=0 gives c=0.c=0c=0. Hence v(x,y)=e−ysin⁡x+12(y2−x2).v(x,y)=\ee^{-y}\sin x+\tfrac12(y^2-x^2).v(x,y)=e−ysinx+21​(y2−x2). Finally we recognize f.ff. Since eiz=e−y+ix=e−y(cos⁡x+isin⁡x)\ee^{\iu z}=\ee^{-y+\iu x}=\ee^{-y}(\cos x+\iu\sin x)eiz=e−y+ix=e−y(cosx+isinx) and −i2z2=xy+i2(y2−x2),-\tfrac{\iu}{2}z^2=xy+\tfrac{\iu}{2}(y^2-x^2)−2i​z2=xy+2i​(y2−x2), f(z)=u+iv=eiz−i2z2,f′(z)=ieiz−iz.f(z)=u+\iu v=\ee^{\iu z}-\frac{\iu}{2}z^2,\qquad f'(z)=\iu\ee^{\iu z}-\iu z .f(z)=u+iv=eiz−2i​z2,f′(z)=ieiz−iz. As a check, Re⁡f′=−e−ysin⁡x+y=ux,\Re f'=-\ee^{-y}\sin x+y=u_xRef′=−e−ysinx+y=ux​, as Proposition 15.6 requires. Every other entire function with real part uuu is f+icf+\iu cf+ic with a real constant c.cc. ◃

The plane is star-shaped, so the theorem applies there. On a set with a hole it can fail, and the failure has a physical meaning.

Example 15.22 (Heat flow through a cylindrical shell). In Lecture 2 the steady temperature in the shell a<r<b,a<r<ba<r<b, with 0<a<b,0<a<b0<a<b, the conductivity κ>0\kappa>0κ>0 and the boundary temperatures Ta≠Tb,T_a\ne T_bTa​=Tb​, is T=Ta+c1ln⁡ra,c1=Tb−Taln⁡(b/a)≠0.T=T_a+c_1\ln\frac ra,\qquad c_1=\frac{T_b-T_a}{\ln(b/a)}\ne0 .T=Ta​+c1​lnar​,c1​=ln(b/a)Tb​−Ta​​=0. It is harmonic on the annulus A={z∈C:a<∣z∣<b}.A=\{z\in\C:a<\abs z<b\}A={z∈C:a<∣z∣<b}. We ask whether it has a harmonic conjugate there, and what such a conjugate would measure.

On the annulus cut along the negative real axis, A∖(−b,−a),A\setminus(-b,-a)A∖(−b,−a), Example 15.13 gives the analytic function f(z)=Ta+c1Log⁡za=Ta+c1(Log⁡z−ln⁡a),f(z)=T_a+c_1\Log\frac za=T_a+c_1(\Log z-\ln a),f(z)=Ta​+c1​Logaz​=Ta​+c1​(Logz−lna), whose real part is T.TT. Its imaginary part V=c1Arg⁡zV=c_1\Arg zV=c1​Argz is a harmonic conjugate on the cut annulus. The level curves of VVV are the rays of Figure 15.1. By Proposition 15.17, ∇T\grad T∇T is orthogonal to ∇V.\grad V∇V. Since ∇V\grad V∇V is normal to the rays, ∇T\grad T∇T and the heat flux j=−κ∇T\vv j=-\kappa\grad Tj=−κ∇T of Lecture 2 are tangent to them.

The conjugate measures the heat flow. Let CCC be a piecewise C1C^1C1 path of GM 40 in the cut annulus, traversed in the direction of increasing parameter. As in GM 41, its unit normal n\vv nn pointing to the right of the direction of travel satisfies n ⁣ds=( ⁣dy,− ⁣dx).\vv n\dd s=(\dd y,-\dd x)nds=(dy,−dx). The heat crossing CCC to the right, per unit time and unit length of the cylinder, is therefore ∫j⋅n ⁣ds=−κ∫(Tx ⁣dy−Ty ⁣dx)=−κ∫(Vy ⁣dy+Vx ⁣dx)=−κ (Vend−Vstart),\int\vv j\cdot\vv n\dd s=-\kappa\int(T_x\dd y-T_y\dd x) =-\kappa\int(V_y\dd y+V_x\dd x)=-\kappa\,\bigl(V_{\mathrm{end}}-V_{\mathrm{start}}\bigr),∫j⋅nds=−κ∫(Tx​dy−Ty​dx)=−κ∫(Vy​dy+Vx​dx)=−κ(Vend​−Vstart​), by the Cauchy–Riemann equations and the gradient endpoint formula of GM 40. Take the arc of the circle of radius rrr from the angle −π+ε-\pi+\varepsilon−π+ε to the angle π−ε,\pi-\varepsilonπ−ε, traversed counterclockwise, with 0<ε<π.0<\varepsilon<\pi0<ε<π. The right of this direction is outward, and VVV changes by 2c1(π−ε)2c_1(\pi-\varepsilon)2c1​(π−ε) along the arc. As ε→0\varepsilon\to0ε→0 the arc fills the whole circle, so the outward power per unit length through the circle is −κ⋅2πc1=2πκ(Ta−Tb)ln⁡(b/a),-\kappa\cdot2\pi c_1=\frac{2\pi\kappa(T_a-T_b)}{\ln(b/a)},−κ⋅2πc1​=ln(b/a)2πκ(Ta​−Tb​)​, the value Q′Q'Q′ of Lecture 2, the same for every radius.

Suppose now that TTT had a harmonic conjugate WWW on the whole annulus. The Cauchy–Riemann equations give Wx=−TyW_x=-T_yWx​=−Ty​ and Wy=Tx.W_y=T_xWy​=Tx​. These derivatives are continuous, so WWW is C1C^1C1 and the gradient endpoint formula applies. This contradicts Q′≠0.Q'\ne0Q′=0. Hence TTT has no harmonic conjugate on the annulus.

The field (−Ty,Tx)=c1(−y,x)/r2(-T_y,T_x)=c_1(-y,x)/r^2(−Ty​,Tx​)=c1​(−y,x)/r2 is c1c_1c1​ times the field of GM 40 that has no potential on the punctured plane. The boundary values of the conjugate c1Arg⁡zc_1\Arg zc1​Argz on the two banks of the cut differ by 2πc1,2\pi c_12πc1​, and Lecture 16 studies this behaviour of the logarithm. ◃

Summary

A function is complex differentiable at z0z_0z0​ exactly when the map (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) of the plane is differentiable there and its derivative is multiplication by f′(z0),f'(z_0)f′(z0​), which the Cauchy–Riemann equations express. The real and imaginary parts of an analytic function with C2C^2C2 parts are harmonic, and on a star-shaped set every harmonic function is such a real part. On an annulus this can fail, as the heat flow through a cylindrical shell shows.

  • Complex derivative: f′(z0)=lim⁡h→0(f(z0+h)−f(z0))/hf'(z_0)=\lim_{h\to0}(f(z_0+h)-f(z_0))/hf′(z0​)=limh→0​(f(z0​+h)−f(z0​))/h over complex h;hh; analytic means complex differentiable on an open set.

  • Cauchy–Riemann: ux=vyu_x=v_yux​=vy​ and uy=−vx,u_y=-v_xuy​=−vx​, necessary at a point; sufficient on an open set when uuu and vvv are C1;C^1C1; f′=ux+ivx.f'=u_x+\iu v_xf′=ux​+ivx​. In polar form ur=vθ/ru_r=v_\theta/rur​=vθ​/r and vr=−uθ/r,v_r=-u_\theta/rvr​=−uθ​/r, with f′=e−iθ(ur+ivr).f'=\ee^{-\iu\theta}(u_r+\iu v_r)f′=e−iθ(ur​+ivr​).

  • Harmonic parts: for analytic fff with C2C^2C2 parts, ∇2u=∇2v=0;\laplacian u=\laplacian v=0∇2u=∇2v=0; where f′≠0f'\ne0f′=0 the level curves of uuu and vvv cross at right angles.

  • Harmonic conjugate: exists on a star-shaped set and is unique up to a constant on a domain; ln⁡r\ln rlnr has the conjugate Arg⁡z\Arg zArgz on the cut plane but none on an annulus about 0.00.

Lecture 16 defines the logarithm and the powers zαz^\alphazα on suitable domains and follows their values along paths that wind around 0.00.

Self-check

4 questions. Answer without looking back at the notes; a first miss gives a hint and a second try. Enter numbers with a decimal point.

1. Suppose f=u+ivf=u+\iu vf=u+iv has continuous first partial derivatives near z0z_0z0​, and the Cauchy–Riemann equations hold at z0z_0z0​. What follows from these assumptions alone?

Hint. What does continuity of the first partial derivatives give for the real differential?

Continuity gives a real differential. At z0z_0z0​ the Cauchy–Riemann equations make that differential multiplication by ux+ivxu_x+\iu v_xux​+ivx​. This gives a derivative for increments in every direction, and the multiplier can be nonzero. Analyticity in a neighbourhood would require complex differentiability throughout that neighbourhood. For example, f(z)=∣z∣2f(z)=\abs z^2f(z)=∣z∣2 satisfies the equations only at zero.

2. Let z=reiθz=r\ee^{\iu\theta}z=reiθ and f(z)=r3cos⁡(3θ)+ir3sin⁡(3θ)f(z)=r^3\cos(3\theta)+\iu r^3\sin(3\theta)f(z)=r3cos(3θ)+ir3sin(3θ) for r>0r>0r>0. Use the radial derivative to find the real part of f′(2i)f'(2\iu)f′(2i). Round to two decimal places.

Hint. At fixed θ\thetaθ, how does zzz change when rrr changes?

The function is the polynomial z3z^3z3, so it is analytic. Along a ray, ∂rz=eiθ\partial_r z=\ee^{\iu\theta}∂r​z=eiθ, which gives f′(z)=e−iθ∂rff'(z)=\ee^{-\iu\theta}\partial_r ff′(z)=e−iθ∂r​f. The radial derivative is 3r2e3iθ3r^2\ee^{3\iu\theta}3r2e3iθ. At r=2r=2r=2 and θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2θ=π/2, the remaining phase is e2iθ=−1\ee^{2\iu\theta}=-1e2iθ=−1. The real part is −12-12−12.

3. Let f=u+ivf=u+\iu vf=u+iv be analytic with C2C^2C2 real and imaginary parts. At a point where f′≠0f'\ne0f′=0, what follows from the Cauchy–Riemann equations?

Hint. Differentiate the equations once for harmonicity. For the angle, compare the two gradients.

The equations give ux=vyu_x=v_yux​=vy​ and uy=−vxu_y=-v_xuy​=−vx​. Equality of mixed partials gives uxx+uyy=vyx−vxy=0u_{xx}+u_{yy}=v_{yx}-v_{xy}=0uxx​+uyy​=vyx​−vxy​=0 and vxx+vyy=−uyx+uxy=0v_{xx}+v_{yy}=-u_{yx}+u_{xy}=0vxx​+vyy​=−uyx​+uxy​=0. Also ∇v=(−uy,ux)\grad v=(-u_y,u_x)∇v=(−uy​,ux​) is a right-angle rotation of ∇u\grad u∇u. Since f′≠0f'\ne0f′=0, both gradients are nonzero. Their level curves have perpendicular normals and cross at right angles.

4. Why does u=ln⁡ru=\ln ru=lnr have no single-valued harmonic conjugate on a full annulus a<r<ba<r<ba<r<b with 0<a<b0<a<b0<a<b, even though it is harmonic there?

Hint. Use the angular derivative of a local conjugate and follow a whole circle.

The polar equations give vθ=rur=1v_\theta=ru_r=1vθ​=rur​=1 and vr=−uθ/r=0v_r=-u_\theta/r=0vr​=−uθ​/r=0, so the local angle θ\thetaθ is a harmonic conjugate. A full turn gives an increase of 2π2\pi2π. A single-valued function must give the same value when the path returns to its starting point, and one additive constant leaves the increase unchanged. The Laplacian of uuu vanishes everywhere in the annulus.
